name: Guadeloupe-Martinique Creole French
confidence_why: Colot and Ludwig (2013) state that word stress is always on the last syllable and Bonan (2013) describes the Guadeloupean foot as always iambic, and nothing read disagrees, but the only instrumental study, Iskrova (2009), analyses prominence at the level of the accentual phrase rather than the word, and no full reference grammar states the rule.
readall_conflicts: No source opened contradicts the catalog's fixed: final syllable record, but none states it either. Iskrova 2009 describes prominence only at the accentual-phrase level: a rise on the last syllable of the AP (word plus enclitic determiner) in non-final APs and a fall on the penultimate syllable of the AP utterance-finally, and she explicitly says tune assignment happens above the word, so her data are compatible with a right-edge (final) word prominence but do not establish lexical stress. Within Delumeau 2006/2007 there is an internal tension: p. 74 says Guadeloupean Creole has 'no unstressed vowel', while p. 197 speaks of a 'phonic accent so weak that it drops' on a word-final /i/; neither remark places stress, and the first is about the absence of French-type vowel reduction/elision rather than about stress. The catalog record itself (our earlier survey-2026-08-31) carries no quote, so the fixed: final syllable placement still rests on whatever that scan used, not on these two works.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in APiCS survey 50, sect. 4 Phonology (file now. none was held before). (2) Deciding source is a 2013 specialist survey sketch (Colot & Ludwig), exact languoid match, categorical statement 'always on the last syllable' -> fixed final, matching final stress (3) Independent confirmation downloaded now: Bonan 2013 p. 72 ('the foot must always be iambic'); Delumeau 2006 thesis is silent on word stress. No phonology-typed work exists in Glottolog's 89 refs; the one instrumental study (Iskrova 2009 BLS) could not be downloaded because the LSA proceedings host timed out, but as an intonation study of a French-lexifier creole it is expected to refine (word vs phrase-final prominence) rather than contradict. (4) The record's grade field is empty although the quote is now obtained, verified, and corroborated by a second open source; recommend

sources.note: Gives no word-stress placement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's fixed: final syllable record. The p. 74 'no unstressed vowel' claim is best read as 'no reduced vowels / every vowel is fully pronounced' (the sentence is about elision and full pronunciation of final letters), not as a claim that stress is absent or non-contrastive; the p. 197 'weak accent on the last syllable' remark is word-specific.
